description: Comprehensive Sociology question bank for Karnataka FDA & SDA Examinations. Covering all topics from the Sociology chapter (Society, Social Institutions, Family, Marriage, Kinship, Community, Social Groups, Socialisation, Social Stratification, Caste, Class, Social Mobility, Urbanisation, Rural Society, Social Change).

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is society?

options.A: A mere collection of people living in one place
options.B: An organised network of social relationships, interactions, institutions, norms and shared ways of life among people
options.C: A political organisation of the state

questions.explanation: Society is an organised network of social relationships, interactions, institutions, norms and shared ways of life among people.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Who described society as a 'web of social relationships'?

options.A: Auguste Comte
options.B: Maclver and Page

questions.explanation: The sociologists Maclver and Page are commonly associated with the description of society as a web of social relationships.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the central basis of society?

options.A: Physical proximity of people
options.B: Social relationships and interaction among individuals

questions.explanation: Social relationships and interaction among individuals are central to society.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Is a mere collection of people living in one place necessarily a society?

options.A: Yes, always
options.B: No, society involves continuing social relationships, interaction, shared norms and organised patterns of life
options.C: Yes, if they speak the same language
options.D: Only if they are related by blood

questions.explanation: A mere collection of people is not necessarily a society; society involves continuing social relationships, interaction, shared norms and organised patterns of life.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a major characteristic of society?

options.A: It is abstract
options.B: It is dynamic
options.D: It is regulated by norms and institutions

questions.explanation: Society is dynamic and continuously changes; it is not static. Major characteristics include being abstract, dynamic, relatively continuous, interdependent, based on social relationships, characterised by similarities and differences, and regulated by norms and institutions.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Why is society considered abstract?

options.A: Because it cannot be seen as a single physical object; it is understood through relationships, institutions, norms and patterns of interaction
options.B: Because it does not exist in reality
options.C: Because it is only a theoretical concept with no practical relevance
options.D: Because it is created by the government

questions.explanation: Society cannot be seen as a single physical object; it is understood through relationships, institutions, norms and patterns of interaction.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Why is society considered dynamic?

options.A: Because it never changes
options.B: Because it continuously changes due to technology, economy, education, migration, political developments, social movements and cultural contact
options.C: Because it is created by nature
options.D: Because it is governed by fixed laws

questions.explanation: Society continuously changes due to technology, economy, education, migration, political developments, social movements and cultural contact.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is social interaction?

options.A: The process through which individuals act and react in relation to one another
options.B: The physical movement of people from one place to another
options.C: The exchange of goods and services only

questions.explanation: Social interaction is the process through which individuals act and react in relation to one another.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What are the two broad forms of social interaction?

options.A: Formal and informal
options.B: Associative and dissociative

questions.explanation: Social interaction may be broadly classified as associative (cooperation, accommodation and assimilation) and dissociative (competition and conflict).

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is cooperation?

options.A: A process in which individuals or groups work together to achieve a common goal
options.B: A process of conflict between groups
options.C: A process of competing for limited resources
options.D: A process of adopting another culture

questions.explanation: Cooperation is a process in which individuals or groups work together to achieve a common goal.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is competition?

options.A: A process in which individuals or groups seek a limited resource, reward or position that cannot be obtained by all
options.B: A process of working together for a common goal
options.C: A process of deliberate opposition between groups

questions.explanation: Competition is a social process in which individuals or groups seek a limited resource, reward or position that cannot be obtained by all.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is conflict?

options.A: A process of working together for a common goal
options.B: A social process involving deliberate opposition or struggle between individuals or groups over interests, values, power or resources
options.C: A process of seeking limited resources
options.D: A process of adjusting to disagreement

questions.explanation: Conflict is a social process involving deliberate opposition or struggle between individuals or groups over interests, values, power or resources.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is accommodation?

options.A: The adjustment of conflicting individuals or groups to reduce or manage disagreement and enable continued interaction
options.B: The process of competing for resources
options.C: The process of adopting another culture
options.D: The process of working together for a common goal

questions.explanation: Accommodation is the adjustment of conflicting individuals or groups to reduce or manage disagreement and enable continued interaction.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is assimilation?

options.A: A process through which individuals or groups gradually adopt elements of another culture and develop shared cultural patterns
options.B: A process of conflict between cultures
options.C: A process of competing for limited resources
options.D: A process of adjusting to disagreement

questions.explanation: Assimilation is a process through which individuals or groups gradually adopt elements of another culture and develop shared cultural patterns.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is social structure?

options.A: The relatively stable, organised pattern of social relationships, statuses, roles, groups and institutions in society
options.B: The physical infrastructure of a society
options.C: The temporary arrangement of people in a crowd
options.D: The biological composition of a population

questions.explanation: Social structure is the relatively stable, organised pattern of social relationships, statuses, roles, groups and institutions in society.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is social function?

options.A: The contribution made by an institution, practice or social pattern to the operation or continuity of a social system
options.B: A ceremony conducted by society
options.C: The physical structure of a society

questions.explanation: A social function is the contribution made by an institution, practice or social pattern to the operation or continuity of a social system.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a social norm?

options.A: A shared rule or expectation that guides behaviour in a particular society or group
options.B: A law passed by the government
options.C: A personal opinion of an individual

questions.explanation: A social norm is a shared rule or expectation that guides behaviour in a particular society or group.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a social value?

options.A: A shared belief about what is desirable, important or worthwhile in a society
options.B: The monetary worth of social institutions
options.C: A law enforced by the state
options.D: A personal preference without social significance

questions.explanation: A social value is a shared belief about what is desirable, important or worthwhile in a society.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is culture?

options.A: The learned and shared way of life of a society, including beliefs, values, norms, language, knowledge, customs, symbols and material objects
options.B: The political system of a society
options.C: The biological characteristics of a population
options.D: The economic organisation of a society

questions.explanation: Culture is the learned and shared way of life of a society, including beliefs, values, norms, language, knowledge, customs, symbols and material objects.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between society and culture?

options.A: Society refers to a network of social relationships; culture refers to the learned way of life shared by people within that network
options.B: Society is biological; culture is political
options.C: Society is static; culture is dynamic
options.D: There is no difference between society and culture

questions.explanation: Society refers primarily to a network of social relationships; culture refers to the learned way of life shared by people within that network.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a social institution?

options.A: An established system of norms, roles, values and practices organised to meet important and recurring social needs
options.B: A physical building where social activities take place

questions.explanation: A social institution is an established system of norms, roles, values and practices organised to meet important and recurring social needs.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT commonly treated as a major social institution?

options.A: Family
options.B: Education

questions.explanation: The family, marriage, kinship, education, religion, economy, polity or government, and law are commonly treated as major social institutions. A commercial bank is an organisation, not a major social institution in the sociological sense.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is a main characteristic of social institutions?

options.A: They are temporary and short-lived
options.B: They are organised, relatively enduring, governed by norms and values, involve statuses and roles, meet social needs, and are transmitted across generations
options.C: They are based purely on individual choice
options.D: They have no connection to social needs

questions.explanation: Social institutions are organised, relatively enduring, governed by norms and values, involve statuses and roles, meet social needs, and are transmitted across generations.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is a primary function of the family as an institution?

options.A: Organising production and distribution of goods
options.B: Reproduction, socialisation, care, emotional support, regulation of sexual relations and transmission of culture

questions.explanation: The family commonly performs reproduction, socialisation, care, emotional support, regulation of sexual relations and transmission of culture.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the role of education as a social institution?

options.A: It organises production and consumption
options.B: It transmits knowledge and skills, socialises individuals, develops capabilities, and helps allocate people to social and occupational positions
options.C: It provides systems of beliefs concerning the sacred

questions.explanation: Education transmits knowledge and skills, socialises individuals, develops capabilities, and helps allocate people to social and occupational positions.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the role of religion as a social institution?

options.A: It organises production and distribution of goods
options.B: It provides systems of beliefs and practices concerning the sacred, creates collective identity and may offer moral guidance, meaning and social solidarity

questions.explanation: Religion provides systems of beliefs and practices concerning the sacred, creates collective identity and may offer moral guidance, meaning and social solidarity.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the role of the economic institution?

options.A: It organises production, distribution, exchange and consumption of goods and services
options.B: It organises power and governance

questions.explanation: The economic institution organises production, distribution, exchange and consumption of goods and services.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the role of political institutions?

options.A: They organise production and consumption
options.B: They organise power, authority, governance, collective decision-making and the maintenance of public order

questions.explanation: Political institutions organise power, authority, governance, collective decision-making and the maintenance of public order.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between an institution and an organisation?

options.A: An institution is an established system of norms and practices, whereas an organisation is a concrete group or structured entity formed to pursue specific objectives
options.B: An institution is a physical building; an organisation is a set of norms
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: An institution is temporary; an organisation is permanent

questions.explanation: An institution is an established system of norms and practices, whereas an organisation is a concrete group or structured entity formed to pursue specific objectives.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is institutionalisation?

options.A: The process through which repeated practices and rules become established, accepted and relatively stable patterns of social life
options.B: The process of building physical institutions
options.C: The process of closing down institutions

questions.explanation: Institutionalisation is the process through which repeated practices and rules become established, accepted and relatively stable patterns of social life.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a manifest function?

options.A: An intended and recognised consequence of a social practice or institution
options.B: An unintended or unrecognised consequence
options.C: A negative consequence of an institution
options.D: A function performed by the government only

questions.explanation: A manifest function is an intended and recognised consequence of a social practice or institution.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a latent function?

options.A: An intended and recognised consequence
options.B: An unintended or unrecognised consequence of a social practice or institution
options.C: A function that is always negative
options.D: A function performed by the family only

questions.explanation: A latent function is an unintended or unrecognised consequence of a social practice or institution.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Who developed the distinction between manifest and latent functions?

options.A: Emile Durkheim
options.B: Max Weber

questions.explanation: Robert K. Merton developed the distinction between manifest and latent functions.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a social dysfunction?

options.A: A positive contribution to social stability
options.B: A consequence of a social arrangement that creates difficulties or undermines the functioning of a social system
options.C: An intended consequence of an institution
options.D: A function performed by the family

questions.explanation: A social dysfunction is a consequence of a social arrangement that creates difficulties or undermines the functioning of a social system.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a family?

options.A: A political organisation
options.B: A socially recognised group commonly connected by marriage, blood, adoption or other recognised ties, with responsibilities such as care, support and socialisation

questions.explanation: A family is a socially recognised group commonly connected by marriage, blood, adoption or other recognised ties, with responsibilities such as care, support and socialisation.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Why is the family called a primary social institution?

options.A: Because it is the largest institution
options.B: Because it is generally the earliest and most influential setting for care, basic learning, emotional development and primary socialisation
options.C: Because it is created by the government

questions.explanation: Family is generally the earliest and most influential setting for care, basic learning, emotional development and primary socialisation.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a major function of the family?

options.A: Reproduction
options.B: Socialisation

questions.explanation: Major functions of the family include reproduction, socialisation, protection, emotional support, economic cooperation, regulation of relationships, care of children and dependent members, and transmission of culture. Conducting elections is a political function, not a family function.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a nuclear family?

options.A: A family that includes grandparents, uncles, aunts and cousins
options.B: A family that generally consists of a couple and their dependent or unmarried children
options.C: A family with only one parent

questions.explanation: A nuclear family generally consists of a couple and their dependent or unmarried children.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is an extended family?

options.A: A family consisting only of a couple and their children
options.B: A family that includes relatives beyond the nuclear unit, such as grandparents, uncles, aunts, cousins or married children
options.C: A family with only one parent

questions.explanation: An extended family includes relatives beyond the nuclear unit, such as grandparents, uncles, aunts, cousins or married children.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a joint family?

options.A: A family with only a couple and their children
options.B: A family arrangement in which two or more related nuclear units, often across generations, live together or maintain a common family organisation and shared responsibilities
options.C: A family with only one parent

questions.explanation: A joint family is a family arrangement in which two or more related nuclear units, often across generations, live together or maintain a common family organisation and shared responsibilities.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a patrilineal family?

options.A: A family that traces descent through the mother's line
options.B: A family that traces descent through the father's line
options.C: A family where authority is vested in women
options.D: A family where the couple lives with the wife's family

questions.explanation: A patrilineal family traces descent through the father's line.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a matrilineal family?

options.A: A family that traces descent through the father's line
options.B: A family that traces descent through the mother's line
options.C: A family where authority is vested in men
options.D: A family where the couple lives with the husband's family

questions.explanation: A matrilineal family traces descent through the mother's line.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a patriarchal family?

options.A: A family in which authority and decision-making are predominantly vested in men, especially senior men
options.B: A family in which women hold predominant authority
options.C: A family that traces descent through the mother's line
options.D: A family where the couple lives with the wife's family

questions.explanation: A patriarchal family is one in which authority and decision-making are predominantly vested in men, especially senior men.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a matriarchal family?

options.A: A family that traces descent through the mother's line
options.B: A family system in which women, especially mothers, hold predominant authority
options.C: A family where the couple lives with the husband's family
options.D: A family with only one parent

questions.explanation: A matriarchal family is a family system in which women, especially mothers, hold predominant authority. It should not be confused with matrilineal descent or matrilocal residence.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is patrilocal residence?

options.A: A post-marital residence pattern in which the couple lives with or near the wife's family
options.B: A post-marital residence pattern in which the couple lives with or near the husband's family
options.C: A post-marital pattern in which the couple establishes a separate household
options.D: A pattern where the couple lives alternately with both families

questions.explanation: Patrilocal residence is a post-marital residence pattern in which the couple lives with or near the husband's family.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is matrilocal residence?

options.A: A post-marital residence pattern in which the couple lives with or near the husband's family
options.B: A post-marital residence pattern in which the couple lives with or near the wife's family
options.C: A post-marital pattern in which the couple establishes a separate household
options.D: A pattern where the couple lives in a joint family

questions.explanation: Matrilocal residence is a post-marital residence pattern in which the couple lives with or near the wife's family.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is neolocal residence?

options.A: A post-marital pattern in which the couple lives with the husband's family
options.B: A post-marital pattern in which the couple lives with the wife's family
options.C: A post-marital pattern in which the couple establishes a separate household
options.D: A pattern where the couple lives with grandparents

questions.explanation: Neolocal residence is a post-marital pattern in which the couple establishes a separate household.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a single-parent family?

options.A: A family in which one parent has primary responsibility for raising one or more children
options.B: A family with a couple and their children
options.C: A family that includes grandparents and cousins

questions.explanation: A single-parent family is a family in which one parent has primary responsibility for raising one or more children.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a blended or reconstituted family?

options.A: A family with only one parent
options.B: A family formed when partners establish a family unit that includes children from one or both partners' previous relationships
options.C: A family that traces descent through the mother's line
options.D: A family where the couple lives with the husband's family

questions.explanation: A blended family is formed when partners establish a family unit that includes children from one or both partners' previous relationships.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is family disorganisation?

options.A: The process of forming a new family
options.B: Disruption in family relationships, roles or functioning, which may arise from conflict, separation, violence, economic stress or other causes
options.C: The expansion of a joint family
options.D: The migration of a family to a new place

questions.explanation: Family disorganisation refers to disruption in family relationships, roles or functioning, which may arise from conflict, separation, violence, economic stress or other causes.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between a nuclear family and a joint family?

options.A: A nuclear family centres on a couple and their children; a joint family includes a wider set of related family members or multiple generations in a shared family arrangement
options.B: A nuclear family includes grandparents; a joint family has only a couple and children
options.C: A nuclear family is always matriarchal; a joint family is always patriarchal
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: A nuclear family centres on a couple and their children; a joint family includes a wider set of related family members or multiple generations in a shared family arrangement.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Is a matrilineal family necessarily matriarchal?

options.A: Yes, always
options.B: No, matrilineal descent concerns the line through which descent is traced; matriarchy concerns the distribution of authority
options.C: Yes, if the family lives in a matrilocal residence

questions.explanation: No. Matrilineal descent concerns the line through which descent is traced; matriarchy concerns the distribution of authority.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is marriage?

options.A: A socially and/or legally recognised union that establishes rights, duties and relationships between spouses and often connects families
options.B: A purely religious ceremony
options.C: A temporary relationship without social recognition

questions.explanation: Marriage is a socially and/or legally recognised union that establishes rights, duties and relationships between spouses and often connects families.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Why is marriage considered a social institution?

options.A: Because it is regulated by social norms, customs, religious practices and laws, and organises recognised spousal relationships and related responsibilities
options.B: Because it is a private matter only
options.C: Because it is a temporary arrangement
options.D: Because it is not recognised by law

questions.explanation: Marriage is regulated by social norms, customs, religious practices and laws, and organises recognised spousal relationships and related responsibilities.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is monogamy?

options.A: A marriage form in which a person has more than one spouse at the same time
options.B: A marriage form in which a person has one spouse at a time
options.C: A marriage form in which one man has more than one wife
options.D: A marriage form in which one woman has more than one husband

questions.explanation: Monogamy is a marriage form in which a person has one spouse at a time.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is polygamy?

options.A: A marriage form in which a person has one spouse at a time
options.B: A marriage form in which a person has more than one spouse at the same time
options.C: A marriage form in which one woman has more than one husband
options.D: A marriage form in which marriage occurs within a caste

questions.explanation: Polygamy is a marriage form in which a person has more than one spouse at the same time.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is polygyny?

options.A: A form of polygamy in which one woman has more than one husband
options.B: A form of polygamy in which one man has more than one wife
options.C: A marriage form in which a person has one spouse at a time

questions.explanation: Polygyny is a form of polygamy in which one man has more than one wife.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is polyandry?

options.A: A form of polygamy in which one man has more than one wife
options.B: A form of polygamy in which one woman has more than one husband
options.C: A marriage form in which a person has one spouse at a time

questions.explanation: Polyandry is a form of polygamy in which one woman has more than one husband.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is fraternal polyandry?

options.A: A form of polyandry in which a woman is married to two or more brothers
options.B: A form of polyandry in which the husbands are not brothers
options.C: A form of polygyny in which one man has more than one wife
options.D: A marriage form in which a person has one spouse at a time

questions.explanation: Fraternal polyandry is a form of polyandry in which a woman is married to two or more brothers.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is non-fraternal polyandry?

options.A: A form of polyandry in which a woman is married to two or more brothers
options.B: A form of polyandry in which the husbands are not brothers
options.C: A form of polygyny in which one man has more than one wife
options.D: A marriage form in which a person has one spouse at a time

questions.explanation: Non-fraternal polyandry is a form of polyandry in which the husbands are not brothers.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is endogamy?

options.A: The rule or practice of marrying outside a specified social group
options.B: The rule or practice of marrying within a specified social group, such as a caste, community or religious group
options.C: Marriage into a group or status considered higher than one's own
options.D: Marriage into a group or status considered lower than one's own

questions.explanation: Endogamy is the rule or practice of marrying within a specified social group, such as a caste, community or religious group.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is exogamy?

options.A: The rule or practice of marrying within a specified social group
options.B: The rule or practice of marrying outside a specified social group
options.C: Marriage into a group or status considered higher than one's own
options.D: Marriage into a group or status considered lower than one's own

questions.explanation: Exogamy is the rule or practice of marrying outside a specified social group.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is hypergamy?

options.A: Marriage into a group or status considered higher than one's own, according to a particular social hierarchy
options.B: Marriage into a group or status considered lower than one's own

questions.explanation: Hypergamy is marriage into a group or status considered higher than one's own, according to a particular social hierarchy.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is hypogamy?

options.A: Marriage into a group or status considered higher than one's own
options.B: Marriage into a group or status considered lower than one's own, according to a particular social hierarchy

questions.explanation: Hypogamy is marriage into a group or status considered lower than one's own, according to a particular social hierarchy.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is an arranged marriage?

options.A: A marriage in which families or intermediaries play a significant role in identifying or negotiating a match; the degree of individual choice varies
options.B: A marriage in which the prospective spouses primarily choose each other based on their relationship
options.C: A marriage solemnised or registered under state law rather than solely through a religious ceremony

questions.explanation: An arranged marriage is one in which families or intermediaries play a significant role in identifying or negotiating a match; the degree of individual choice varies.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a love marriage?

options.A: A marriage in which families play the primary role in choosing a match
options.B: A marriage in which the prospective spouses primarily choose each other based on their relationship, although family involvement may also occur
options.C: A marriage registered under state law

questions.explanation: A love marriage is one in which the prospective spouses primarily choose each other based on their relationship, although family involvement may also occur.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is civil marriage?

options.A: A marriage solemnised through a religious ceremony only
options.B: A marriage solemnised or registered under state law rather than solely through a religious ceremony

questions.explanation: Civil marriage is a marriage solemnised or registered under state law rather than solely through a religious ceremony.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between monogamy and polygamy?

options.A: Monogamy involves one spouse at a time; polygamy involves more than one spouse at the same time
options.B: Monogamy involves more than one spouse; polygamy involves one spouse
options.C: Monogamy is marriage within a caste; polygamy is marriage outside a caste
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: Monogamy involves one spouse at a time; polygamy involves more than one spouse at the same time.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between endogamy and exogamy?

options.A: Endogamy requires or favours marriage within a specified group; exogamy requires or favours marriage outside that group
options.B: Endogamy requires marriage outside a group; exogamy requires marriage within a group
options.C: Endogamy is marriage between relatives; exogamy is marriage between strangers
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: Endogamy requires or favours marriage within a specified group; exogamy requires or favours marriage outside that group.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the Special Marriage Act, 1954?

options.A: An Indian law providing a civil form of marriage for persons irrespective of religion, subject to the Act's legal conditions and procedures
options.B: An Indian law governing marriage among Hindus only
options.C: An Indian law prohibiting child marriage
options.D: An Indian law regulating divorce only

questions.explanation: The Special Marriage Act, 1954 is an Indian law providing a civil form of marriage for persons irrespective of religion, subject to the Act's legal conditions and procedures.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955?

options.A: An Indian law providing a civil form of marriage for persons irrespective of religion
options.B: An Indian law governing marriage among persons to whom the Act applies, including provisions concerning conditions for a valid marriage, ceremonies, restitution, judicial separation, divorce and related matters
options.C: An Indian law prohibiting child marriage
options.D: An Indian law regulating the registration of births and deaths

questions.explanation: The Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 is an Indian law governing marriage among persons to whom the Act applies, including provisions concerning conditions for a valid marriage, ceremonies, restitution, judicial separation, divorce and related matters.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006?

options.A: An Indian law providing a civil form of marriage for persons irrespective of religion
options.B: An Indian law governing marriage among Hindus
options.C: An Indian law intended to prohibit child marriages and provide legal remedies and penalties
options.D: An Indian law regulating divorce among all communities

questions.explanation: The Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006 is an Indian law intended to prohibit child marriages and provide legal remedies and penalties. The statutory age definitions and legal consequences should be studied from the current Act.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006, what is the definition of a child?

options.A: A male who has not completed 18 years and a female who has not completed 16 years
options.B: A male who has not completed 21 years and a female who has not completed 18 years
options.C: A male who has not completed 18 years and a female who has not completed 21 years

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is kinship?

options.A: A system of socially recognised relationships based on descent, marriage, adoption or other culturally recognised ties
options.B: A system of political relationships only
options.D: A legal system of property inheritance

questions.explanation: Kinship is a system of socially recognised relationships based on descent, marriage, adoption or other culturally recognised ties.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What are the two major bases of kinship?

options.A: Consanguineal and affinal kinship
options.B: Patrilineal and matrilineal kinship

questions.explanation: The two major bases of kinship are consanguineal kinship, based on descent or socially recognised blood relations, and affinal kinship, based on marriage.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is consanguineal kinship?

options.A: Relationships created through marriage
options.B: Relationships understood as arising through descent, such as parent-child and sibling relationships

questions.explanation: Consanguineal kinship refers to relationships understood as arising through descent, such as parent-child and sibling relationships.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is affinal kinship?

options.A: Relationships understood as arising through descent
options.B: Relationships created through marriage, such as relationships between spouses and in-laws

questions.explanation: Affinal kinship refers to relationships created through marriage, such as relationships between spouses and in-laws.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is descent?

options.A: The socially recognised tracing of a person's ancestry and group membership through specified lines of parentage
options.B: The movement of people from one place to another
options.C: The process of marriage outside one's group

questions.explanation: Descent is the socially recognised tracing of a person's ancestry and group membership through specified lines of parentage.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is patrilineal descent?

options.A: Descent traced through the female line
options.B: Descent traced through the male line
options.C: Descent traced through both the mother's and father's lines

questions.explanation: Patrilineal descent traces ancestry and descent-group membership through the male line.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is matrilineal descent?

options.A: Descent traced through the male line
options.B: Descent traced through the female line
options.C: Descent traced through both the mother's and father's lines

questions.explanation: Matrilineal descent traces ancestry and descent-group membership through the female line.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is bilateral descent?

options.A: Descent traced only through the male line
options.B: Descent traced only through the female line
options.C: Descent that recognises kinship through both the mother's and the father's lines

questions.explanation: Bilateral descent recognises kinship through both the mother's and the father's lines.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a lineage?

options.A: A descent group whose members claim descent from a common ancestor who may be legendary or not individually known
options.B: A descent group whose members trace their relationship to a known common ancestor
options.C: A group formed through marriage only

questions.explanation: A lineage is a descent group whose members trace their relationship to a known common ancestor.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a clan?

options.A: A descent group whose members trace their relationship to a known common ancestor
options.B: A descent group whose members claim descent from a common ancestor, who may be legendary or not individually known
options.C: A group formed through marriage only

questions.explanation: A clan is a descent group whose members claim descent from a common ancestor, who may be legendary or not individually known.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a nuclear or elementary family in kinship terminology?

options.A: The basic family unit consisting of spouses and their children
options.B: A family that includes grandparents and cousins
options.C: A family with only one parent

questions.explanation: A nuclear or elementary family in kinship terminology is the basic family unit consisting of spouses and their children.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a kinship terminology system?

options.A: A legal system of inheritance
options.B: The culturally established vocabulary used to classify and address relatives, such as mother, uncle, cousin and in-law

questions.explanation: A kinship terminology system is the culturally established vocabulary used to classify and address relatives, such as mother, uncle, cousin and in-law.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is preferential marriage?

options.A: A culturally favoured marriage pattern with a particular category of relative or group, where permitted by that society's rules
options.B: A marriage arranged by the government
options.C: A marriage that is legally prohibited
options.D: A marriage based on love only

questions.explanation: Preferential marriage refers to a culturally favoured marriage pattern with a particular category of relative or group, where permitted by that society's rules.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a cross-cousin?

options.A: The child of a parent's same-sex sibling, such as a father's brother's child or a mother's sister's child
options.B: The child of a parent's opposite-sex sibling, such as a mother's brother's child or a father's sister's child
options.C: A cousin related through marriage only
options.D: A cousin from the same village

questions.explanation: A cross-cousin is the child of a parent's opposite-sex sibling, such as a mother's brother's child or a father's sister's child.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a parallel cousin?

options.A: The child of a parent's opposite-sex sibling, such as a mother's brother's child or a father's sister's child
options.B: The child of a parent's same-sex sibling, such as a father's brother's child or a mother's sister's child
options.C: A cousin related through marriage only
options.D: A cousin from the same village

questions.explanation: A parallel cousin is the child of a parent's same-sex sibling, such as a father's brother's child or a mother's sister's child.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between lineage and clan?

options.A: A lineage generally traces descent from a known common ancestor; a clan claims common descent, often from an ancestor whose exact identity may be unknown or symbolic
options.B: A lineage claims descent from an unknown ancestor; a clan traces descent from a known ancestor
options.C: A lineage is based on marriage; a clan is based on blood
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: A lineage generally traces descent from a known common ancestor; a clan claims common descent, often from an ancestor whose exact identity may be unknown or symbolic.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a community?

options.A: A group of people connected by a sense of belonging and shared social life, commonly associated with a locality, common interests or identity
options.B: A political party

questions.explanation: A community is a group of people connected by a sense of belonging and shared social life, commonly associated with a locality, common interests or identity.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is a main characteristic of a community?

options.A: A sense of belonging, social interaction, shared interests or identity, continuity and some form of common life
options.B: Formal written rules only

questions.explanation: A community commonly involves a sense of belonging, social interaction, shared interests or identity, continuity and some form of common life.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between community and society?

options.A: A community is usually a more bounded group with a sense of belonging; society is the wider network of social relationships and institutions
options.B: A community is wider than society
options.C: Society is a bounded group; community is the wider network
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: A community is usually a more bounded group with a sense of belonging; society is the wider network of social relationships and institutions.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a rural community?

options.A: A community situated in a countryside or village setting, often characterised by lower population density and a significant role for agriculture or allied activities, though rural economies are diverse
options.B: A community located in a city with high population density
options.C: A community that exists only online
options.D: A community formed by the government

questions.explanation: A rural community is a community situated in a countryside or village setting, often characterised by lower population density and a significant role for agriculture or allied activities, though rural economies are diverse.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is an urban community?

options.A: A community situated in a countryside or village setting
options.B: A community located in a town or city, typically characterised by higher population density, occupational diversity and complex institutions
options.C: A community that exists only online

questions.explanation: An urban community is a community located in a town or city, typically characterised by higher population density, occupational diversity and complex institutions.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a neighbourhood?

options.A: A local area in which residents interact and may develop shared identity, mutual support and common concerns
options.B: A political party

questions.explanation: A neighbourhood is a local area in which residents interact and may develop shared identity, mutual support and common concerns.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a community association?

options.A: A voluntary or organised body formed by residents or members to address shared local interests
options.B: A government department

questions.explanation: A community association is a voluntary or organised body formed by residents or members to address shared local interests.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is community sentiment?

options.A: The feeling of belonging, attachment and shared identity among members of a community
options.B: A legal document forming a community
options.D: An economic transaction within a community

questions.explanation: Community sentiment is the feeling of belonging, attachment and shared identity among members of a community.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a virtual community?

options.A: A community located in a village
options.B: A group whose members interact and develop shared interests or identity primarily through digital communication platforms
options.C: A community formed by the government

questions.explanation: A virtual community is a group whose members interact and develop shared interests or identity primarily through digital communication platforms.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a social group?

options.A: A collection of people who interact, share some sense of membership and are connected by social relationships or common interests
options.B: A collection of people who share a characteristic but never interact

questions.explanation: A social group is a collection of people who interact, share some sense of membership and are connected by social relationships or common interests.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is an essential feature of a social group?

options.A: Interaction, mutual awareness, shared norms or interests, a sense of belonging, and some degree of organisation or continuity
options.B: Physical proximity only

questions.explanation: Essential features of a social group include interaction, mutual awareness, shared norms or interests, a sense of belonging, and some degree of organisation or continuity.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Who introduced the concepts of primary and secondary groups?

options.A: Max Weber
options.B: Charles Horton Cooley

questions.explanation: Charles Horton Cooley introduced the concepts of primary and secondary groups.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a primary group?

options.A: A relatively small group characterised by intimate, personal, face-to-face and enduring relationships
options.B: A large formal organisation with impersonal relationships
options.D: A group based on shared characteristics but no interaction

questions.explanation: A primary group is a relatively small group characterised by intimate, personal, face-to-face and enduring relationships.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is an example of a primary group?

options.A: A university
options.B: A government department
options.C: Family, close friendship groups and intimate neighbourhood groups

questions.explanation: Family, close friendship groups and intimate neighbourhood groups are common examples of primary groups.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a secondary group?

options.A: A relatively small group with intimate and personal relationships
options.B: A generally larger and more formal group, with relationships that are often impersonal, specialised and goal-oriented
options.D: A group based on shared characteristics but no interaction

questions.explanation: A secondary group is generally larger and more formal, with relationships that are often impersonal, specialised and goal-oriented.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following can function as a secondary group?

options.A: Family
options.B: Close friendship group
options.C: A university, government department, trade union, business organisation and professional association

questions.explanation: A university, government department, trade union, business organisation and professional association can function as secondary groups.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is an in-group?

options.A: A group that a person perceives as outside their own group
options.B: A group with which a person identifies and to which the person feels a sense of belonging
options.C: A group used as a standard for evaluating attitudes
options.D: A group with deliberately established rules

questions.explanation: An in-group is a group with which a person identifies and to which the person feels a sense of belonging.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is an out-group?

options.A: A group with which a person identifies and feels a sense of belonging
options.B: A group that a person perceives as outside their own group, sometimes with feelings of distance or opposition
options.C: A group used as a standard for evaluating attitudes
options.D: A group with deliberately established rules

questions.explanation: An out-group is a group that a person perceives as outside their own group, sometimes with feelings of distance or opposition.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Who is associated with the concepts of in-group and out-group?

options.A: Charles Horton Cooley
options.B: William Graham Sumner

questions.explanation: William Graham Sumner is associated with the concepts of in-group and out-group.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a reference group?

options.A: A group that an individual uses as a standard for evaluating attitudes, behaviour, values or aspirations
options.B: A group with which a person identifies and feels belonging
options.C: A group perceived as outside one's own group
options.D: A group with deliberately established rules

questions.explanation: A reference group is a group that an individual uses as a standard for evaluating attitudes, behaviour, values or aspirations.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Who developed the concept of reference groups in modern sociology?

options.A: Charles Horton Cooley
options.B: William Graham Sumner

questions.explanation: Robert K. Merton made an influential contribution to reference-group theory.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a formal group?

options.A: A group that develops through personal relationships and spontaneous interaction
options.B: A group that has deliberately established rules, roles, procedures and objectives
options.D: A group based on shared characteristics but no interaction

questions.explanation: A formal group has deliberately established rules, roles, procedures and objectives.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is an informal group?

options.A: A group with deliberately established rules and procedures
options.B: A group that develops through personal relationships and spontaneous interaction rather than a formally prescribed structure
options.D: A group based on shared characteristics but no interaction

questions.explanation: An informal group develops through personal relationships and spontaneous interaction rather than a formally prescribed structure.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a voluntary group?

options.A: A group into which membership is assigned or into which a person is born
options.B: A group that individuals join by choice, such as a cultural association or charitable organisation
options.D: A group based on shared characteristics but no interaction

questions.explanation: A voluntary group is one that individuals join by choice, such as a cultural association or charitable organisation.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is an involuntary group?

options.A: A group that individuals join by choice
options.B: A group into which membership is assigned or into which a person is born, such as a family of birth
options.D: A group based on shared characteristics but no interaction

questions.explanation: An involuntary group is one into which membership is assigned or into which a person is born, such as a family of birth.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a social aggregate?

options.A: A collection of people who interact and share a sense of membership
options.B: A collection of people in the same place or situation who may not share lasting interaction or group identity
options.C: A classification of people who share a characteristic but do not interact
options.D: A formal organisation with written rules

questions.explanation: A social aggregate is a collection of people in the same place or situation who may not share lasting interaction or group identity.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a social category?

options.A: A collection of people who interact and share a sense of membership
options.B: A collection of people in the same place or situation who may not share lasting interaction
options.C: A classification of people who share a characteristic, even if they do not interact or identify as a group
options.D: A temporary gathering of people responding to a shared event

questions.explanation: A social category is a classification of people who share a characteristic, even if they do not interact or identify as a group.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a crowd?

options.A: A collection of people who interact and share a sense of membership
options.B: A temporary gathering of people in a common physical setting, often responding to a shared event or stimulus
options.C: A classification of people who share a characteristic but do not interact
options.D: A formal organisation with written rules

questions.explanation: A crowd is a temporary gathering of people in a common physical setting, often responding to a shared event or stimulus.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between a social group and a social category?

options.A: Members of a social group interact and have a sense of membership; members of a social category share a characteristic but may never interact
options.B: Members of a social group never interact; members of a social category always interact
options.C: A social group is always larger than a social category
options.D: There is no difference between them

questions.explanation: Members of a social group interact and have a sense of membership; members of a social category share a characteristic but may never interact.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is socialisation?

options.A: The lifelong process through which individuals learn and internalise the norms, values, roles, language and behaviour patterns of their society
options.B: A temporary process limited to childhood
options.C: The process of formal education only

questions.explanation: Socialisation is the lifelong process through which individuals learn and internalise the norms, values, roles, language and behaviour patterns of their society.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Why is socialisation important?

options.A: It develops social identity, teaches cultural expectations, enables communication, prepares people for social roles and supports social continuity
options.B: It is only important for children
options.C: It has no role in social continuity
options.D: It is limited to formal education

questions.explanation: Socialisation develops social identity, teaches cultural expectations, enables communication, prepares people for social roles and supports social continuity.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Who is associated with the concept of the looking-glass self?

options.A: George Herbert Mead
options.B: Charles Horton Cooley

questions.explanation: Charles Horton Cooley is associated with the concept of the looking-glass self.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the looking-glass self?

options.A: Cooley's idea that a person's self-concept develops partly through imagining how others see and judge them and responding to those imagined evaluations
options.B: Mead's idea about the generalised other

questions.explanation: The looking-glass self is Cooley's idea that a person's self-concept develops partly through imagining how others see and judge them and responding to those imagined evaluations.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Who developed the theory of the social self through role-taking and play?

options.A: Charles Horton Cooley
options.B: George Herbert Mead

questions.explanation: George Herbert Mead developed the theory of the social self through role-taking and play.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: In Mead's theory, what is the 'I'?

options.A: The organised set of attitudes and expectations of others that the individual has internalised
options.B: The spontaneous and initiating aspect of the self
options.C: The internalised understanding of the broader community's attitudes

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: In Mead's theory, what is the 'Me'?

options.A: The spontaneous and initiating aspect of the self
options.B: The organised set of attitudes and expectations of others that the individual has internalised
options.C: The biological instinct of an individual
options.D: The internalised understanding of the broader community's attitudes

questions.explanation: The 'Me' is the organised set of attitudes and expectations of others that the individual has internalised.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the generalised other in Mead's theory?

options.A: The spontaneous aspect of the self
options.B: The internalised understanding of the broader community's attitudes, rules and expectations
options.C: A specific individual who influences socialisation
options.D: A formal organisation with written rules

questions.explanation: The generalised other is the internalised understanding of the broader community's attitudes, rules and expectations.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is primary socialisation?

options.A: The learning of roles and expectations in settings beyond the early family environment
options.B: The early and foundational learning of language, basic norms, values and behaviour, commonly within the family
options.C: Learning the values and behaviour associated with a role a person expects to enter
options.D: Replacing previously learned norms and behaviour patterns

questions.explanation: Primary socialisation is the early and foundational learning of language, basic norms, values and behaviour, commonly within the family.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is secondary socialisation?

options.A: The early and foundational learning within the family
options.B: The learning of roles and expectations in settings beyond the early family environment, such as schools, workplaces and peer groups
options.C: Learning the values associated with a role a person expects to enter
options.D: Replacing previously learned norms and behaviour patterns

questions.explanation: Secondary socialisation is the learning of roles and expectations in settings beyond the early family environment, such as schools, workplaces and peer groups.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is resocialisation?

options.A: The early and foundational learning within the family
options.B: The learning of roles and expectations in settings beyond the early family environment
options.C: Learning the values associated with a role a person expects to enter
options.D: The process of replacing or substantially modifying previously learned norms, values and behaviour patterns

questions.explanation: Resocialisation is the process of replacing or substantially modifying previously learned norms, values and behaviour patterns.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a socialisation agent?

options.A: A person, group or institution that influences the learning of social norms and behaviour
options.B: A government law

questions.explanation: A socialisation agent is a person, group or institution that influences the learning of social norms and behaviour.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following are major agents of socialisation?

options.A: Family, peer groups, schools, religion, mass media, workplace, community and digital media
options.B: Only the family

questions.explanation: Major agents of socialisation include family, peer groups, schools, religion, mass media, workplace, community and digital media.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Why is family considered the first agent of socialisation?

options.A: Because it is the largest institution
options.B: Because it usually provides the earliest sustained interaction through which children learn language, basic norms, values, habits and social roles
options.C: Because it is created by the government

questions.explanation: Family usually provides the earliest sustained interaction through which children learn language, basic norms, values, habits and social roles.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the role of peer groups in socialisation?

options.A: They transmit formal knowledge and teach discipline
options.B: They influence identity, communication, cooperation, fashion, attitudes, independence and behaviour through interaction among people of similar age or status
options.C: They circulate information and cultural representations
options.D: They provide the earliest sustained interaction for children

questions.explanation: Peer groups influence identity, communication, cooperation, fashion, attitudes, independence and behaviour through interaction among people of similar age or status.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the role of schools in socialisation?

options.A: They influence identity and fashion through peer interaction
options.B: They transmit formal knowledge and also teach discipline, punctuality, cooperation, competition, citizenship and institutional rules
options.C: They circulate information and cultural representations
options.D: They provide the earliest sustained interaction for children

questions.explanation: Schools transmit formal knowledge and also teach discipline, punctuality, cooperation, competition, citizenship and institutional rules.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the role of mass media in socialisation?

options.A: They transmit formal knowledge and teach discipline
options.B: They influence identity through peer interaction
options.C: They circulate information, values, cultural representations and behavioural models that can influence public attitudes and individual conduct
options.D: They provide the earliest sustained interaction for children

questions.explanation: Mass media circulate information, values, cultural representations and behavioural models that can influence public attitudes and individual conduct.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is the difference between socialisation and education?

options.A: Education is an organised process of learning, often through formal institutions; socialisation is broader and includes formal and informal lifelong learning of social life
options.B: Socialisation is limited to schools; education is lifelong
options.C: There is no difference between them
options.D: Education is informal; socialisation is formal

questions.explanation: Education is an organised process of learning, often through formal institutions; socialisation is broader and includes formal and informal lifelong learning of social life.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Is socialisation completed in childhood?

options.A: Yes, it ends with childhood
options.B: No, socialisation continues throughout life as people enter new roles, institutions and social environments
options.C: Yes, it ends after primary school

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is social stratification?

options.A: The structured and relatively enduring ranking of individuals and groups in a society, producing unequal access to resources, power, prestige and opportunities
options.B: The equal distribution of resources in society
options.D: The temporary arrangement of people in a crowd

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is a major basis of social stratification?

options.B: Only income

questions.explanation: Class, caste, gender, race or ethnicity, occupation, wealth, power, education and status can shape social stratification.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Which of the following is a main characteristic of social stratification?

options.A: It is temporary and random

options.C: It is based purely on individual effort
options.D: It is the same in all societies

questions.explanation: Social stratification is socially structured, hierarchical, relatively persistent, involves unequal rewards and opportunities, and varies across societies and historical periods.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is social inequality?

options.A: The equal distribution of resources among all people
options.B: Unequal distribution of resources, opportunities, rights, power or rewards among individuals and groups
options.D: The temporary arrangement of people in a crowd

questions.explanation: Social inequality refers to unequal distribution of resources, opportunities, rights, power or rewards among individuals and groups.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is an open system of stratification?

options.A: A system that restricts movement between social positions
options.B: A system that permits comparatively greater movement between social positions, often through education, occupation, income or achievement
options.C: A system based only on birth
options.D: A system with no social positions

questions.explanation: An open system permits comparatively greater movement between social positions, often through education, occupation, income or achievement.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a closed system of stratification?

options.A: A system that permits great movement between social positions
options.B: A system that restricts movement between social positions and assigns status largely by birth or inherited membership
options.C: A system based only on achievement
options.D: A system with no social positions

questions.explanation: A closed system restricts movement between social positions and assigns status largely by birth or inherited membership.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is ascribed status?

options.A: A social position acquired through an individual's actions and efforts
options.B: A social position assigned to an individual largely at birth or without personal choice
options.C: The expected behaviour associated with a social status
options.D: The recognised position an individual occupies within a social structure

questions.explanation: Ascribed status is a social position assigned to an individual largely at birth or without personal choice.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is achieved status?

options.A: A social position assigned at birth
options.B: A social position acquired through an individual's actions, efforts, qualifications or accomplishments
options.C: The expected behaviour associated with a social status
options.D: The recognised position an individual occupies within a social structure

questions.explanation: Achieved status is a social position acquired through an individual's actions, efforts, qualifications or accomplishments.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is social status?

options.A: The expected behaviour associated with a particular social status
options.B: The recognised position an individual occupies within a social structure
options.C: A social position assigned at birth
options.D: A social position acquired through effort

questions.explanation: Social status is the recognised position an individual occupies within a social structure.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: What is a social role?

options.A: The recognised position an individual occupies within a social structure
options.B: The expected behaviour associated with a particular social status
options.C: A social position assigned at birth
options.D: A social position acquired through effort

questions.explanation: A social role is the expected behaviour associated with a particular social status.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: Who explained class stratification through economic relations and ownership of the means of production?

options.A: Max Weber
options.B: Karl Marx

questions.explanation: Karl Marx explained class stratification through economic relations and ownership of the means of production.

questions.subject: Sociology
questions.question: In Marx's analysis of capitalism, what are the two major social classes?

options.A: The upper class and the middle class
options.B: The bourgeoisie, who own or control the means of production, and the proletariat, who sell their labour power
options.D: The capitalists and the middle class
